Hello everyone, welcome to Best Partners , I’m Da Fei. Let me start with a question: if you were standing inside an economic bubble right now, do you think you could get out before it bursts? Don't be too quick to answer. The past 400 years of financial history show that almost everyone inside a bubble says " yes," and that is exactly what makes a bubble so dangerous. Recently, Edward Chancellor, author of "Devil Take the Hindmost: A History of Financial Speculation," joined Wilfred Frost’s podcast to systematically compare historical financial manias with the current AI craze. Published in 1999, the. book is still considered an authoritative study on the subject today , and Chancellor himself has worked in the investment industry for many years. This interview was packed with information, so I’ve summarized the key takeaways for you. First, regarding his underlying perspective: Chancellor comes from a background in history, and he believes speculation cannot be understood through economics alone—it must be viewed within its social context . In the 1840s, Charles Mackay wrote a book that grouped financial events like Tulip Mania, the Mississippi Scheme, and the South Sea Bubble alongside social. frenzies like witch hunts. This arrangement in itself tells us something . In Chancellor’s view, financial speculative mania is just social mania occurring in the economic sphere, driven by human nature that hasn't changed much in centuries. The starting point of this logic is the dividing line between investing and gambling. There is a profound quote from a 1930s book about Wall Street titled "Where Are the Customers 'Yachts?" The author, Fred Schwed, wrote that "speculation is an effort to turn a little money into a lot , which usually fails, while investment is the effort to prevent a lot of money. from becoming a little, which usually succeeds." Simply put, investing is about protecting your principal, maintaining a margin of safety, and accepting slow accumulation of returns, while speculation is betting to make a quick buck. The core characteristic of a bubble is that most people in the market have shifted from being investors to gamblers. Schwed also observed that in a speculative bubble, risk is mispriced, so the returns on these bets eventually turn out to be very poor. Looking at the massive trading volumes on retail platforms today, many people think they are investing, but they are either.

gambling outright or making speculative bets. If we turn the clock back to the early 17th century in the Netherlands— the first modern commercial society— that was when both bond and stock markets first took shape. The Dutch East India Company paid dividends and stocks were traded, then a bubble suddenly appeared in tulips. It is said that at the time, a rare tulip bulb that could bloom with variegated petals was worth as much as a townhouse in Amsterdam. Tulips were indeed rare, but behind this was a classic feedback effect; people kept bidding up prices, buying more the higher they went. By the mid-1630s, Dutch interest rates were very low,. foreign capital flooded in, and tulips even developed a futures market. Low interest rates, leverage, and capital inflows—these are the standard ingredients of a bubble. What's interesting is how this bubble ended; there was no clear trigger because trading had shifted entirely to futures , and the gap between futures and spot prices reached such an extreme that it collapsed on its own without any spark. After the collapse, the authorities intervened and simply voided these contracts. In the 1690s, there was another, lesser-known mania in England. At the time, a shipwreck was salvaged. off the coast of Massachusetts, earning investors huge profits, which led to the first technological mania: diving bells . Money was extremely loose, and the first newspapers publishing stock prices appeared then, giving speculative sentiment a medium to spread for the first time. One figure from this period is worth mentioning: Richard Steele, a journalist, writer, playwright, and also an entrepreneur. He wrote half-jokingly that stock price fluctuations were just like the height of ladies' hairstyles, both illustrating how speculative sentiment rises and falls like fashion. He wrote a quote that has been cited repeatedly ever since, to the effect. that nothing is more useful than deeply understanding people's hopes and fears: stay cautious when others are jubilant, and buy with quiet joy when others think it's in their interest to sell. Sounds familiar, right? This is the original version of "be greedy when others are fearful." Chancellor says that if you want to be a serious investor, understanding these few lines is enough . This story has an ironic ending: Steele himself later participated in a company involved in the South Sea Bubble , a fish-farming venture it seems. The first person to fully articulate contrarian investing couldn't avoid falling into the mania himself, so who.

can laugh at whom? Speaking of the South Sea Bubble, that was a very short but massive bubble in 1720. There is a mindset here that is particularly worth pondering; in finance, it's called " Greater Fool Theory"—I am willing to buy at a price higher than the fundamental value because I believe you are a greater fool who will take it off my hands. There was a banker back then who once said, "Since the whole world is mad , we must follow suit; may the devil take those who fall behind." The title of Chancellor's book comes directly from this quote. You see, those in the midst of a frenzy aren't all just hot-headed; they enter with a calculated nonchalance , hoping to escape before things go wrong. Yet, the banker who said this eventually lost everything, claiming he had been misled. After a frenzy ends, almost everyone who lost money looks for a scapegoat; this was especially typical after the South Sea Bubble burst. You might ask yourselves if this script looks familiar. The host asked a very sharp question: today, this is politely referred to in the industry as " momentum investing." Isn't chasing gains and fleeing losses essentially just a rebranded version of gambling? And from the lows of 2009 to now, this trick has. worked for nearly 20 years. Chancellor responded calmly, noting that momentum as a factor, backtested in the U.S. to the 1920s, has historically provided a few percentage points of excess return, especially during times of mania. But he once saw a study showing that from 1995 to 2015, you couldn't make any money at all using momentum. Over the past 10 to 15 years, momentum has been exceptionally strong. One reason is the market's shift from active to passive investing; fund managers who underperform are fired, and capital flows into indices, pouring into the large-cap stocks that are already rallying. Another reason is the massive. community of retail traders in the U.S. , whose trading volume may be double that of professional investors, and these people are naturally inclined to buy whatever is rising. In his words, it works—until the day it doesn't. The most poignant comparison in this interview is about the key players in the bubble. The South Sea Bubble had a central figure named Sir John Blunt, a company director and the main architect of the entire affair. Chancellor described him as having an exaggerated, commanding style , a sense of boundless power; listen to this description and see if it resonates with the major figures in today's boom.

Chancellor himself draws exactly this analogy. Jensen Huang wants to position Nvidia as an indispensable company for the AI revolution, and Nvidia has been providing funds to some shaky data center firms, engaging in massive vendor financing—it's a bit like the telecom boom at the turn of the century, but on a much larger scale. And if you believe that humanity is heading toward AGI, or that superintelligence is the main narrative—an almost inevitable destination—then for people like Sam Altman at OpenAI or Elon Musk at SpaceX , Thaler argues they need to instill an almost religious faith in what they are. doing to raise the funds to get it done . He added a restrained remark: not every bubble requires a messianic leader , but having such an individual makes the mania run more efficiently. Moreover , these leaders eventually tend to cross the line, because flattery and adoration are themselves part of the feedback loop . People are naturally prone to becoming overconfident. Blount was like that back then; he crossed the line, providing leverage to South Sea stock buyers through his own Sword Blade Bank and bribing Parliament, the King, and the Prince of Wales. As an aside regarding a bit of etymological trivia: back then,. the word "bubble" meant fraud. A bubble was a scam, so the South Sea Bubble, understood in its original sense, was a massive fraud. There is also a sequel to the South Sea Bubble that is worth mentioning. After 1720, Britain passed retroactive legislation that directly confiscated the wealth people had earned during the bubble. The grand estate in Yorkshire bought by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Aislabie was seized, and the money that the family of historian Edward Gibbon thought they had earned legally was also taken away. By British legal standards, this was extremely rare , which shows just how fierce the political backlash was at the time. Thaler connects this history to the present: financial manias require authorities to turn a blind eye, or even actively support them. In his view, Trump has played this role over the past few years, launching cryptocurrencies named after himself with unusually frequent account trading, his family participating in various projects, and real estate deals conveniently closing wherever his diplomats flew. And analysis after the midterm elections showed that the public was extremely dissatisfied with the corruption of this administration—or rather, what they perceived as corruption. Can this prick the bubble? Thaler says anything could cause the bubble to burst, yet stock.

prices remain high; if this bubble does burst, it will be much more violent than anything we have seen so far. Next is the railway bubble of the 1840s, which is the most similar comparison to today . People at the time were all talking about the railway bubble, discussing it in public, yet the bubble still burst. This serves as a reminder for today; during a recent market dip, mainstream media on both sides of the ocean were asking if there was an AI bubble. Many people feel that since everyone is discussing it to this extent, the market will probably surge for another wave. The lesson of the railway bubble is precisely that when it finally bursts,. people may have known it was a bubble all along. People’s excitement about railways back then was identical to the excitement for AI today; they said railways would bring world peace and that everyone would speak the same language. By the way, people in AI are saying the same thing today, and perhaps with even more reason. Excess capital was poured in; three lines were built from London to Peterborough, and three from Leeds to Manchester—purely redundant construction. It was the same with the fiber-optic information superhighway in the early 21st century, and it’s the same with AI today, as countless similar models compete and data centers are built one after another. . Some have crunched the numbers, factoring in planned investments over the next five years, and AI infrastructure spending could reach $ 15 trillion—by this metric, it's even bigger than the railway mania of the past. However, Chancellor warns that just because someone points out a bubble doesn’t mean it will burst immediately, because the momentum behind it can be extremely strong. There is another pattern that has run through 400 years of bubble history: every time communication technology advances, speculation accelerates along with it. In the late 17th century, there were newspapers; in the railway age, the telegraph; in the 1920s, radio, telephones, and ticker machines; in the. 90s, the internet connected everyone. The 2020–2021 meme stock bubble was driven by Reddit’s WallStreetBets, which could only happen in a hyper-connected world. Chancellor says this also helps explain why cryptocurrency speculation has persisted so long; contagious speculative ideas can spread across the globe in an instant. He shared his own observations: he lives most of the time in Somerset, quite a remote place, and he was surprised to see people in the village trading AI stocks and cryptocurrencies. People there should have used that money to buy land, so why were they buying tokens instead? That is why the line he wrote years ago.

resonates even more deeply today. The more connected we are and the more information we possess, the less rational our behavior and the worse our decisions become. This judgment applies not only to finance but also to politics —in a highly interconnected world, irrationality always rushes to the forefront. Moral hazard is another core concept in Chancellor’s book. The section on the Japanese bubble reads today almost as if it were describing the current US market. In the 1980s, skeptics were told that the Japanese government wouldn't let stock prices fall, and that Japanese banks and brokerages were too big to fail. After the bubble burst, this belief was proven. to be a destructive, illusory fantasy. The bubble burst when the Bank of Japan raised interest rates; Governor Yasushi Mieno intended to prick it, and he succeeded, taking the stock market over 30 years to recover. China's real estate bubble followed the same script; despite 50 million vacant apartments and irrational valuations, people insisted Beijing wouldn't let it burst, until the "three red lines" policy in late 2020 restricted developer credit. The essence of moral hazard, as Chanos puts it, is simple: if the upside is yours but you don't bear the downside, you will naturally take more risks. So, where is. the greatest danger in the AI frenzy? Chanos believes this may be the most dangerous investment mania in history because the technical path is uncertain ; Nvidia currently holds a dominant position, but it is not the only player , with Google and Broadcom building TPUs and China developing competitive products. The real issue is that no one knows which technology will ultimately win, as many believe we will shift from massive models requiring data centers the size of half of Manhattan to small models that run in an office or even on a phone. If that happens, we likely won't need as many chips. On the model. side, things are also unclear, as OpenAI's models continue to lose market share to open-source competitors. There is a saying that you can achieve 95%of the performance at just 2%of the cost. Unless one is mindlessly scaling, those who truly want to control costs only use frontier models when absolutely necessary, opting for cheaper competing products otherwise. This situation feels familiar; during the internet boom, those providing access ended up in a commoditized business nobody cared about —between 1999 and 2000, Freeserve held 17%of the UK market, but who cares about them now? There were too many mobile.

operators, too many access providers, and too much fiber laid down; those new telecom companies could never overcome the economic hurdles. Today, independent data center providers might face the same fate. This is the most thought-provoking moment of the entire interview. When a bubble hits its peak, the market cannot distinguish the ultimate winners because a crash follows ; looking back at the internet, those who talked about an internet revolution were generally right—it changed everyone's life and was a civilizational information revolution. Yet, except for Amazon—whose stock price fell about 95% at the time—the real winners emerged. later; Google hadn't gone public, and Facebook hadn't even been founded. Sylar's view is that you can observe the emergence of revolutionary technologies , but generally speaking, it makes more sense to take a step back, wait for the bubble to burst, see how the industry reshuffles, and then see which companies are gaining dominance. Perhaps the AI sector will see a repeat of this scene. Anyway, Sylar finally discussed why he thinks the "Everything Bubble" is back, referring to the analytical framework investor Richard Bernstein wrote in 2021 ; leverage, trading volume, the democratization of finance, and IPOs— all these factors are present now. SpaceX completed the largest IPO in history, and in his view, it can also be seen as the largest meme stock in history. Data from brokerage firms show that the U.S. stock trading volume in the summer of 2026 was even higher than the peak in 2021; the number of retail clients is several times what it used to be, and business has expanded from meme stocks to cryptocurrencies and prediction betting, with leverage everywhere. Some betting platforms have turned to perpetual futures, where leverage can perhaps reach 100x or 200x , and there are also 3x leveraged ETFs tracking Nvidia and SK Hynix. The most frenzied scene actually appeared in. South Korea, where retail investors calling themselves "ants" used leverage to speculate on semiconductor stocks, with the Korean Prime Minister even publicly supporting it; moral hazard appeared again, so what is the biggest difference this time compared to history ? Sylar believes it is the government's fiscal base; the U.S. government had a fiscal surplus in the 1920s, and also in 1999 to 2000. Studying financial crises , debt levels were relatively low, so the authorities had the ability to step in and clean up, giving moral hazard room to play. But things are different now; countries like the UK, US, and France, which rely heavily on foreign borrowing and international investment.

positions, owe more to the rest of the world than the overseas assets they own . Japan is an exception; its outstanding debt is indeed the highest, but it also holds the world's largest overseas assets, which is a support. So when this situation unravels, what happens within government debt is well worth watching. When will this bubble burst? The indicators Sylar gave sound a bit boring . After capital tightens and interest rates rise, the bursting of bubbles is very common in history. The Federal Reserve began raising rates in 1928, eventually making margin loan costs unsustainable, leading to the 1929 crash ; the Bank of Japan raised rates in 1989. ; Greenspan's Fed was also raising rates in 1999 and 2000; the U.S. housing bubble was inflated during the ultra-low interest rate period after the dot-com era. It began to burst after the Fed raised rates consecutively in 2004, so his point is that the main feature when a speculative bubble bursts is a capital crunch. The current situation is a bit awkward. U.S. interest rates are much higher than five years ago, offering decent real yields on inflation-protected bonds, while comparable equity yields are much lower . The equity risk premium, as the academics call it, has all but vanished . However, he added that from 1999 to 2000, real yields on U.S. inflation-protected securities reached 4.5%while the stock market was at its most expensive level ever, suggesting these trends could potentially go even further. If you aren't worried about the government's long-term ability to repay debt, then trimming some equity positions and shifting more into bonds would be much more reasonable. Throughout the interview, Thaler's stance was clear: it walks like a bubble , it talks like a bubble—no matter how you look at it, it’s a bubble. But he doesn't predict timing, and admits that investors are always proven wrong; however, this should help everyone calibrate their judgment and avoid being overconfident. Finally, the host asked. him what the most important investment advice for the audience was. His answer was somewhat unexpected: avoid passive or index investing. In his view, indexation has gone too far. The indices themselves are too concentrated, specifically in the most speculative themes. It makes more sense to entrust your money to investors who actually judge fair value. Over 400 years of bubbles, the scripts have changed countless times, but human nature hasn't changed a single act. Returning to the opening question, if history shows that winners only emerge after the shuffle, do you still believe you’re the one who can exit the game early? Thanks for.

watching, and see you next time. y.

摘要

泡沫裡的人，總以為自己能及時離場

作者以一個問題開場：若身處經濟泡沫之中，人們是否能在泡沫破裂前脫身？回顧四百年金融史，身在泡沫中的人幾乎都相信自己辦得到，而這種自信正是泡沫危險之處。作者整理了《魔鬼取後：金融投機史》作者愛德華・錢斯勒接受訪談的觀點，指出投機狂熱不能只從經濟學理解，也必須放回社會脈絡中觀察；金融市場的瘋狂，其實是人性在經濟領域的集體狂熱。

投資與投機的界線

錢斯勒引用費瑞德・施維德對投資與投機的區分：投機是想用少量資金換取大量財富，通常以失敗告終；投資則是避免大量財富縮水，通常較能成功。投資重視本金保護、安全邊際與長期累積；投機則追求快速獲利。泡沫的核心特徵，是市場參與者逐漸從投資者變成賭徒，風險價格被扭曲，下注的預期報酬最終往往很差。如今許多散戶自認在投資，實際上卻可能是在賭博或進行高度投機。

從鬱金香狂熱到南海泡沫

十七世紀荷蘭的鬱金香狂熱，出現在低利率、外國資金湧入與鬱金香期貨興起的環境中。稀有球莖價格被不斷推高，買家因價格上漲而更願意買進，形成典型的正向回饋循環。泡沫崩潰時並沒有明確導火線，期貨與現貨價格的落差已大到難以維持，市場於是自行瓦解，當局事後則作廢相關契約。

十七世紀末的英國也曾因打撈沉船獲利而掀起潛水鐘投機熱潮；當時貨幣寬鬆，報紙開始刊載股價，讓投機情緒有了傳播媒介。記者理查・斯蒂爾曾把股價波動比作女士髮型的流行起落，也提出在眾人狂喜時保持謹慎、在他人想賣出時冷靜買進的逆向思維。然而，斯蒂爾後來自己也參與了南海泡沫相關企業，顯示即使懂得逆向投資道理，也未必能免於群體狂熱。

1720年的南海泡沫則呈現了「更大的傻瓜理論」：買家明知價格高於基本價值，仍相信可以轉手給出價更高的人。一名銀行家甚至認為既然全世界都瘋了，就必須跟著瘋，書名《魔鬼取後》也源自這種心態。錢斯勒提醒，泡沫參與者不一定只是頭腦發熱；不少人自認十分理性，只是盤算著在出事前離場。可是，鼓吹這套說法的人最後也可能血本無歸，而泡沫破裂後，受害者往往急著尋找代罪羔羊。

動能交易何時失靈

訪談將歷史狂熱連結到今日的「動能投資」：追逐上漲標的、避開下跌標的，是否只是重新包裝的賭博？錢斯勒指出，動能策略在美國歷史資料中曾帶來額外報酬，但不同時期表現差異很大，甚至有研究顯示某些年份區間幾乎無利可圖。近十多年動能特別強勢，部分原因是資金從主動投資轉向被動指數投資，推升已經上漲的大型股；另一部分原因則是散戶交易量龐大，投資者容易追買正在上漲的股票。這種策略「有效，直到它不再有效」。

泡沫領袖、人工智慧與政治回聲

南海泡沫的重要推手約翰・布朗特，憑藉強勢姿態與無所不能的自信主導公司計畫，後來更透過自己的銀行向買家提供槓桿，並賄賂政要。錢斯勒將這類領袖與當前人工智慧熱潮中的重要人物相提並論：輝達希望成為人工智慧革命不可或缺的公司，也曾以供應商融資支持財務狀況不穩的資料中心業者；而相信通用人工智慧或超級智慧必將到來的人，則需要以近乎宗教式的信念說服投資者投入巨額資金。錢斯勒認為，泡沫不一定需要救世主式領袖，但這類人物能讓狂熱更有效率；掌聲與吹捧也會形成回饋循環，使領袖更容易越界。

「泡沫」一詞在當時也帶有欺詐之意。南海泡沫破裂後，英國甚至追溯立法，沒收部分人在泡沫中取得的財富，顯示政治反彈之強烈。錢斯勒進一步指出，金融狂熱往往需要當局視而不見，甚至提供支持；他以近年美國政壇與加密貨幣、家族商業計畫等爭議作為當代聯想，並提到民眾對政府腐敗疑慮的不滿。訪談最後追問，這類政治反彈是否足以刺破泡沫；提供的內容在問題提出後便告中止，未呈現後續回答。
